method: Blind solves recorded from the blind files in verification/blind-read-u1-fix/ only, before opening any file under questions/. MCQ picks are single letters. SAQ answers are my own words from the stimulus. LEQ entries are my own thesis + outline scored against the blind rubric.

apush-saq-0001.a: One characteristic is variety: the Americas held large cities such as Cahokia, empires such as the Aztec and the Inca, and many smaller farming and hunting societies, each adapted to its own region.
apush-saq-0001.b: Portuguese sailing down the African coast taught Europeans to use Atlantic winds and currents, and the search for a sea route to Asian spices gave them a reason to sail west, so by 1492 Europeans had both the skill and the motive to cross the ocean.
apush-saq-0001.c: European arrival brought conquest and forced labor, and it also brought diseases such as smallpox to peoples with no immunity, so Indigenous populations fell sharply and many societies lost people, land, and political independence.

apush-saq-0002.a: Columbus claims that the islands are full of gentle people who are quick to learn, and that the islands hold gold and spices worth seeking.
apush-saq-0002.b: Columbus wrote to report his voyage to the Spanish court and to win support for more voyages, so he stressed the people, the gold, and the spices to show that the voyage had paid off and deserved further backing.
apush-saq-0002.c: The letter shows what Columbus wanted the court to hear, not how Indigenous peoples saw themselves, because Columbus describes them briefly as gentle and quick to learn in order to praise the voyage, and he spent only weeks among them.

apush-saq-0003.a: One feature is the coast of South America on the left side of the map, drawn as a long green coastline facing the Atlantic, beside the Caribbean islands.
apush-saq-0003.b: The map shows that by 1502 Europeans knew the shape of Africa, the Atlantic, and the eastern coast of South America, but they had mapped only the Atlantic side of the Americas, so their knowledge was still shaped by the voyages made so far.
apush-saq-0003.c: The north-south line through the Atlantic marks the division of new lands between Spain and Portugal under the Treaty of Tordesillas, and the small flags along the coasts mark which crown claimed each shore, so the map records competition as well as geography.

apush-saq-0004.a: The arid Southwest led the Pueblo peoples to farm dry land and build adobe villages.
apush-saq-0004.b: Maize farming in the fertile river valleys produced surpluses that fed dense populations, and those surpluses supported chiefs, priests, and the labor that raised the mounds.
apush-saq-0004.c: Both the Pueblo peoples and the Iroquois villagers were farming peoples living in settled villages.

apush-saq-0016.a: The engraving shows Spanish soldiers torturing bound Indigenous people over a fire, presenting Spanish rule as violent and cruel toward the people it governed.
apush-saq-0016.b: Las Casas wrote to persuade the Spanish crown to stop the cruelty he described; his account was an appeal for reform of the encomienda system, not a neutral report.
apush-saq-0016.c: De Bry never visited the Americas, so he drew what he imagined from Las Casas's text. The image also served a European audience that wanted to see Spanish cruelty, so it may exaggerate what it shows.

apush-leq-0001.thesis: Contact brought massive change to the Americas — disease, conquest, forced labor, and the Columbian Exchange — but continuities persisted in Indigenous resistance, adaptation, and surviving cultures, languages, and farming practices.
apush-leq-0001.outline: Context: diverse Indigenous societies before 1492; European motives for overseas expansion. Evidence of change: smallpox and the 50-90 percent population decline; conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires; encomienda and repartimiento forced labor. Evidence of continuity: Indigenous resistance and adaptation; surviving cultures, languages, and trade and farming practices. Analysis: change was profound but uneven by region and group; complexity: qualify the thesis by region.

apush-leq-0002.thesis: Environment shaped how Native societies adapted: Pueblo peoples dry-farmed and built adobe villages in the arid Southwest, Iroquois peoples practiced three sisters farming in the Northeast woodlands, and Chinook peoples built fishing villages on the Pacific coast.
apush-leq-0002.outline: Context: diversity of Native societies before 1492; maize spread from Mexico across North America. Evidence 1: Pueblo dry farming and adobe villages in the Southwest. Evidence 2: Iroquois three sisters farming in the Northeast; Chinook fishing villages on the Pacific coast. Analysis: all adapted food systems to their environments, but the forms differed sharply. Complexity: similar environments still produced different societies, and adaptation also transformed the land.

apush-leq-0003.thesis: Maize agriculture transformed many Native societies greatly, letting cities like Cahokia and Tenochtitlan grow large on surpluses, but the transformation was limited where maize did not spread or was not adopted.
apush-leq-0003.outline: Context: maize first grown in Mesoamerica thousands of years ago, spreading north. Evidence of transformation: Cahokia growing to about 20,000 people on maize surpluses; Tenochtitlan feeding about 200,000. Evidence of limits: Plains peoples hunting bison on foot; Chinook villages built on fishing rather than farming. Analysis: compare maize-farming societies with societies that did not depend on maize. Complexity: maize enabled change but did not determine every outcome.

apush-leq-0004.thesis: Economic motives were the leading cause of European exploration from 1492 to 1607, but religion and rivalry shaped where and how exploration happened.
apush-leq-0004.outline: Context: the search for Asian trade, the Reconquista, Portugal's African voyages. Evidence: the spice trade; Spanish silver; the Treaty of Tordesillas and joint-stock companies. Analysis: economics led while religion and rivalry shaped the course of exploration.

apush-leq-0008.thesis: Ancestry largely determined a person's place in Spanish colonial society, fixing legal rank and social standing, but the determination was not total: mixing kept producing new categories that outran the labels.
apush-leq-0008.outline: Context: Spanish rule built on conquest and forced labor; the encomienda system; the Spanish concern with pure blood. Evidence: peninsulares and criollos, one or two percent of the population, held the top offices; Indians and Africans stood at the bottom. Evidence: the separate legal republics of Spaniards and Indians, with offices, tribute, and legal standing assigned by birth. Analysis: ancestry set the rank while mixing kept producing new categories.

apush-leq-0011.thesis: Disease was the leading cause of Spanish success, doing more than any other single factor to break Native resistance, but it was not the only cause: steel, horses, and Native allies mattered too.
apush-leq-0011.outline: Context: Spanish arrival in 1492 and the conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires; the Columbian Exchange moving people, goods, and germs. Evidence: smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in late 1520, before the siege, killing the emperor Cuitlahuac and weakening the defense; Native populations fell 50 to 90 percent between 1500 and 1650; the Americas had been separated from Old World germs for thousands of years, so there was no immunity. Analysis: disease did the most damage, but it worked with war, enslavement, and the breakdown of food systems.
